newsitem.title: USA: Soybean, coffee prices soar on tight supply.
newsitem.headline: Soybean, coffee prices soar on tight supply.

text.p: Soybean prices soared Monday on worries that heavy demand from processors and exporters might eat up already tight supplies before an expected big harvest this fall.
Coffee prices renewed their strong rally, also on worries about supplies. But oil prices fell on worries about too much supply.
The Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau of 17 commodity futures ended up 1.82 points at 247.19.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, May soybeans closed up the allowable 30-cent per bushel daily trading limit at $8.60, the highest closing price since Sept. 23, 1988.
May soybean meal also closed up the $10 per ton daily limit at $275.70, and May soybean oil closed up 0.64 cent per pound at 26.33 cents.
The day's furious buying came ahead of a monthly report by the Agriculture Department due Tuesday.

"The report, if it comes out as expected, will add more fuel to the fire," said Vic Lespinasse, trader with Dean Witter. "The market has a job to do. It has to ration supply and it's trying to do just that."
Analysts expect the department to cut its projection of U.S. soybean stocks for next Sept. 1 by 10 million to 15 million bushels Tuesday from 140 million bushels last month.
That estimate was itself down 15 million bushels from the department's January estimate and compared with 183 million bushels on hand last year and 335 million two years agao.
"This just shows the explosive nature of this market," said Dave Armstrong, analyst with ABN-AMRO Chicago Corp.
Expected big South American soybean crops now being harvested have become less important than record demand from domestic processors, he said.
Powered by the rally in soybeans, corn jumped to 5-1/2 month highs, with May corn up 5-3/4 cents a bushel at $3.09-3/4. May wheat closed up up 3-3/4 cents at $3.79-1/4.
At the Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, March coffee futures shrugged off early weakness and rose 9.75 cents to 215.50 cents a pound, up 108 percent since the rally started on Dec. 9.

"Basically, it keeps rising on the reality of short supply," said Refco Inc. analyst Ann Prendergast. "And apprehensiveness of: 'Can I get the coffee I need?' No one has experienced any relief on the prospect of tight stocks."
After the market's close, leading coffee roaster Folgers said it would raise the list price on its standard 13-ounce can by 15 cents immediately due to higher cash coffee prices.
The increase, bringing the new price for a standard can to $2.86, came only a week after a 45-cent increase Folgers earlier posted took effect.
Precious metals also ended sharply higher as gold proved resilient enough to stave off further dips below $350.00.
"In the last couple of trading days gold was unable to get much down past support at $350.00, and silver held its ground quite nicely," analyst Edward Kempf of the CPM group said.
April gold at the New York Mercantile Exchange's Comex division closed $3.20 an ounce higher at $353.10. May silver ended 9.0 cents higher at $5.275.

Some traders drew comfort from comments by Hans Tietmeyer, president of Germany's central bank, that he had heard of no central banks planning gold sales since the Swiss announced their plan last week to raise cash for a new Holocaust fund. Central bank sales have weighed heavily on gold prices this year.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, oil prices closed lower as a flood of imports from Europe and West Africa put a halt to the recent recovery in prices.
April crude oil closed down 79 cents a barrel at $20.49. April gasoline closed 1.31 cents a gallon lower at 64.36 cents and April heating oil fell 1 cent to 53.08 cents a gallon.

"This all has to do with a lot imports coming over from Europe, where there are a lot of refiners in maintenance . . . and poor market margins," said Al Lindseth, a trader with GSC Energy in Atlanta, who also cited imports from Nigeria.
